principles.title: Symmetric placement on the flatcar's longitudinal axis
principles.principle: The vehicle must be centered on the flatcar's longitudinal axis; left/right track (or wheel) overhang past the flatcar sides must be equal, differing by no more than 40mm.
principles.purpose: Even weight distribution across both bogies of the flatcar.
principles.physics: Asymmetric loading shifts load onto one rail/bogie, increasing derailment risk on curves and uneven track, and causing uneven wheel-rail wear.
principles.engineeringReason: Keeps the flatcar's own center of gravity close to its designed centerline under dynamic (braking, curving) loads.
principles.militaryRequirement: Mandatory for all six approved tracked-vehicle securing methods.

principles.title: Vehicle immobilized before securing (parking brake + reverse gear)
principles.principle: Once positioned, the vehicle's transmission is left in reverse gear and the parking brake is applied before fastening begins.
principles.purpose: Prevents the vehicle from creeping forward during the securing process and adds a passive resistance to forward movement in transit.
principles.physics: A braked drivetrain converts translational force at the wheel/track contact patch into resisted torque at the transmission, reducing the load the chocks/lashings alone must react.
principles.engineeringReason: Redundant restraint — the securing hardware is sized assuming the brake may not hold under all conditions, not as the sole restraint.
principles.militaryRequirement: Required step in the sequence for all six methods.

principles.title: Chocks placed at the second-from-last road wheel
principles.principle: For chock-based methods (1 and 2), the chocking hardware is positioned where the track meets the ground just ahead of the second-to-last road wheel — not at the very end of the track run.
principles.purpose: This is the point of maximum, most stable ground contact under the track, minimizing the chance the vehicle rides up and over the chock under braking loads.
principles.physics: Placing a stop at a point of sustained (rather than momentary) ground pressure resists both the vehicle's forward momentum and any tendency to climb the obstacle.
principles.engineeringReason: A chock placed at a point of lighter contact pressure (e.g., directly under the idler wheel) is more likely to be crushed or ridden over.

principles.title: Wire lashing strand count scales with angle, not just load
principles.principle: The number of wire strands in a lashing is selected from a lookup table (Table 7) based on the angle between the lashing and the flatcar's longitudinal axis AND the angle between the lashing and the flatcar floor — steep or shallow angles both require more strands than a mid-range angle.
principles.purpose: A lashing at a poor angle carries less of its rated tension as useful restraining force.
principles.physics: Only the force component along the direction of expected vehicle movement (roughly longitudinal) actually resists that movement; a lashing running nearly parallel to the direction of travel, or nearly vertical, wastes most of its tension on components that don't resist forward/lateral sliding, so more strands compensate for the lost efficiency.
principles.engineeringReason: Rather than requiring field crews to compute vector components, the handbook pre-solves the geometry into a lookup table.
principles.militaryRequirement: Table 7 is mandatory input for method 3 (tracked) and method 2 (wheeled) wire lashings.

principles.title: Some hardware is restricted to named vehicle types
principles.principle: Iron spurs (Table 13), iron stop-boots (Table 11), and the MK-765/S-765 clamp system are not general-purpose — each is only approved for the specific vehicle/object designations listed against it.
principles.purpose: These items are shaped to match a specific track-link, road-wheel, or hull geometry.
principles.physics: A stop designed for one track-link profile may not seat correctly, or may not distribute load correctly, on a different vehicle's running gear.
principles.engineeringReason: Cross-using vehicle-specific hardware risks it slipping, cracking under load, or failing to engage the track/wheel at all.
principles.militaryRequirement: Table 13 lookup is mandatory before selecting a spur; substitution outside the listed vehicle set is not authorized by the handbook text available.

principles.title: Hardware quantity scales with vehicle weight bracket
principles.principle: The wire-lashing count for wheeled vehicles doubles once combat weight crosses 24 t (4 lashings up to 24t, 8 lashings 24.1-40t). Reusable chock system variant likewise changes with weight bracket.
principles.purpose: Heavier vehicles impart more kinetic energy in the same deceleration event, requiring proportionally more restraint.
principles.physics: Restraining force needed scales with mass (F = m*a for a given assumed deceleration during braking/shunting impact).
principles.engineeringReason: Rather than a continuous formula, the handbook uses discrete weight brackets tied to standardized hardware sets, so no in-field computation is required.
principles.militaryRequirement: Weight bracket lookup is mandatory before hardware selection (Tables 8, 9, 15).
